description: We’re building “Dancing with the SARs” for NASA Space Apps 2026—a Multi-SAR platform turning satellite radar data into clear insights on environmental change. I focus on Next.js, frontend, architecture, and data science. We’re looking for teammates in GIS/remote sensing, Python/data science, AI/ML, UI/UX, research, and backend. If you’re curious, collaborative, and ready to build, join us!
summary:
During monsoon floods and severe riverbank erosion, thick cloud cover and darkness blind optical satellites when communities need monitoring most. At the same time, raw Synthetic Aperture Radar (SAR) imagery requires complex orbit-track matching, calibration, and threshold tuning that keep radar data out of reach for non-specialists.

TerraPulse addresses the "Dancing with the SARs" challenge by turning open radar observations into an accessible, transparent web platform for tracking surface change. It combines 10 precomputed Copernicus Sentinel-1 C-band case studies (covering flood inundation, riverbank erosion, deforestation, and wetland dynamics across Bangladesh and global sites) with a 10-date NASA-ISRO NISAR L-band GCOV provisional time series over Hakaluki Haor.

Instead of relying on a single cutoff, TerraPulse tests every measurement across a threshold range to display uncertainty bounds—such as the 2022 Sylhet flood extent of 37.19 km² (tested range 30.85–44.01 km²) paired with WorldPop 2020 gridded population exposure estimates. Users can also pick any custom area on an interactive map to query live NASA ASF pass availability, generate single-orbit Google Earth Engine export scripts, and listen to results through Chiku, a built-in voice guide.
details:
TerraPulse is an interactive web platform that makes radar satellite observations understandable for non-specialists. It answers the "Dancing with the SARs" challenge by letting anyone compare two dates and see where the surface changed, even under monsoon clouds and at night, when optical satellites cannot see.

What it does: TerraPulse includes 10 precomputed Copernicus Sentinel-1 C-band case studies (flood inundation, riverbank erosion, deforestation and wetland dynamics across Bangladesh and global sites) and a 10-date NASA-ISRO NISAR L-band GCOV provisional time series over Hakaluki Haor. Instead of trusting a single threshold, every measurement is tested across a threshold range, so users see uncertainty bounds, for example the 2022 Sylhet flood extent of 37.19 km2 (tested range 30.85 to 44.01 km2), paired with WorldPop 2020 population exposure estimates. Users can also select any custom area on the map to check live NASA ASF pass availability, generate single-orbit Google Earth Engine export scripts, and listen to results through Chiku, a built-in voice guide.

Impact: Relief teams, planners, researchers and students can read radar change without learning orbit matching, calibration or threshold tuning. The tool reports observations with uncertainty, not forecasts.

Tools: Next.js web app with a Python processing pipeline, Google Earth Engine, Sentinel-1, NISAR GCOV, NASA ASF, WorldPop, deployed on Vercel.

Creativity: The threshold-range uncertainty display, the population-exposure pairing and the voice guide make radar results transparent and accessible.
